winningClaim.title: Organic engagement, engineered reach: @clipsbykes is a paid per-view clipper (866-video audit)
winningClaim.description:
Verdict: the likes, saves and comments on the Gunna clip look organic, with no bot signature (about 80% confidence). But the reach is engineered, so the clip is not proof of "massive Kimchi popularity".

New evidence that no other claim has:

1) The account is a paid per-view clipper. Content Rewards (Whop's clipping marketplace) lists "Orangie's Campaign" by "Memecoin Clippers (orangie)": $1 per 1k views, 13 Aug to 30 Sep 2026. Its top 5 clips are @clipsbykes posts. Clipper "kesv1" ranks #1 with 49 approved clips, 3.1M paid views and $2,647 earned.

2) Same footage, other uploaders. Another account's upload of the SAME Gunna scene runs 1,017 likes per comment. A same-vlog clip on @clipsbykes runs 1,889:1. So the target's ~915:1 follows the content and does not prove bought likes.

3) Time test, using Rasmr's own screenshot. At hour 15 (48.8K likes, 56 comments, 2,305 saves) the clip had 4.72 saves per 100 likes. At hour 73 it has 4.70. Day-3 viewers liked 8.5% of 46,832 new plays, against 8.6% lifetime. A like package would have shifted both.

4) Full catalog: all 866 videos, where other claims used 3 to 60. Every metric sits within 1.3 sd of the account's own log-log fit.

5) Comments are not frozen. They are at 102 now. At our pull, the 101 were exactly 58 top-level comments + 43 replies. Commenter accounts have a median age of 3.2 years (decoded from user IDs) and come from 15 countries.

6) A same-day flood. In the 24 h after the vlog, 40+ other accounts posted 57+ Kimchi clips, and 6 of them used one identical caption. Two of the three most-liked comments mock Kimchi.

Limits: TikTok's private analytics are not public, and a drip-fed package that buys likes, saves and comments in natural proportions cannot be fully excluded.

Full report, CSV data and scripts: https://github.com/swiftbotlab/research-notes/tree/main/tiktok-clipsbykes-kimchi

claims.title: Organic reach, no bot signature: 45-video baseline + 96 comments on the @clipsbykes Kimchi clip
claims.description:
Short answer: no evidence of bought views or bought likes. The one genuinely low metric is comments, and it is a content-format effect that reproduces inside the same account.

METHOD. 45 videos from @clipsbykes' public profile grid (2026-03-04 .. 10-20, 69.09M views) with views, likes, comments, shares and saves; exact counters, because logged-out TikTok rounds big numbers to 2-3 significant figures (43 of 45 view counters end in 00); the "48k likes in 11 hours" screenshot in the original X post as an independent earlier reading; 48 top-level comments + 48 replies with author region and like counts.

THE DECISIVE TEST. Hour 11 -> day 5 (2026-10-26 02:45 UTC): likes 48,800 -> 101,088 (+107.1%), comments 56 -> 114 (+103.6%), saves 2,305 -> 4,728 (+105.1%). Likes per comment 871 -> 887; saves per like 4.72% -> 4.68%. The engagement added after hour 11 alone (52,288 likes / 58 comments) is 902:1 with 4.63% saves per like - i.e. slightly FEWER comments per like than the lifetime average. A purchased early package predicts the opposite. Views are still ticking (+45 in 124 seconds), not frozen at a delivered bundle.

BASELINE. The account: 29,500 followers, 872 videos, 6.2M lifetime likes, "Daily clips". In the 45-video sample 11 videos passed 1M views (median 401,900, best 24.1M), so 1.18M is ordinary here. The clip's like rate is 8.56% vs a 5.81% account median - 60th percentile. Not inflated.

THE REAL ANOMALY. Comments per like: 0.113% vs 1.17% account median (p10 0.32%) - the lowest of 45. It tracks video format, not traffic source: how-to/DIY clips on the same account run 36.0% and 4.9%; spectacle clips run 0.16-0.27% (its Monaco car clip: 1.1M views, 18.7% like rate, 0.16% comments). The account's other Kimchi clips: 0.19%, 0.32%, 0.68%, 0.87%, 1.17%. A 26-second flex clip with nobody to argue with lands where the account's spectacle clips land.

MEASUREMENT NOTE. Logged-out counters are rounded to 2-3 significant figures (43 of 45 view counters end in 00, only 7 of 45 comment counters do), so the 871:1 / 906:1 / 937:1 spread across readings is noise of about 1.6% on the numerator, not evidence that anything changed.

COMMENTS ARE HUMAN. 48 distinct accounts, zero repeated handles, top comment 2,083 likes, 41 of 48 with likes, commenters from 8+ countries (NG 17, US 10, GB 7, ZA 4, GH 2, CA 2...), on-topic slang ("Kimchi larped his homies earnings", "his coin went crazy i got in so early too", "where is the vlog??"). Four of 48 are crypto promo spam - the opposite of bought praise.

AND NO, THIS IS NOT A TIKTOK FANBASE. 1.18M views on 29.5k followers is For-You distribution, 40x the follower base; the video is a reposted clip, the audience is a general spectating one. "1.1M views" does not measure Kimchi's pull.

Limits: no view snapshots before hour 11; 96 of 114 comments captured; commenter follower counts are not exposed publicly.

Full audit with tables, all 45 videos, all comments and the raw JSON: https://9xj89gzrtw-hue.github.io/kimchi-clip-audit/ (data: https://github.com/9xj89gzrtw-hue/kimchi-clip-audit)

claims.title: Not organic as presented: likes inflated vs. comments/shares on @clipsbykes
claims.description:
Verdict: the cited video has a real audience underneath it, but its likes are out of line with everything else viewers did. The pattern fits purchased likes/views layered on real traffic, timed to the coin's run.

1) One-day burst. On Oct 21 @clipsbykes posted 12 Kimchi clips in 18 hours. They pulled 2.63M of the 2.98M plays across the account's 24 newest videos (88%). The next day plays fell off a cliff: none of the 10 later clips reached 40K, and two sit at ~1-2K.

2) Likes up, everything else down. Per 1,000 plays (before / Oct 21 / after):
- likes 58.9 / 75.6 / 35.7
- shares 4.6 / 1.5 / 0.8
- comments 0.68 / 0.17 / 0.50
Real viewers who like more also comment and share more. Here only likes rose.

3) The cited video: 1.2M plays, 99.7K likes, 112 comments = 890 likes per comment. The median Oct 21 clip has 385 likes per comment, later clips 41, and the pinned clips 79-100.

4) No follower lift. Followers went from 28.1K to 28.8K (Oct 20-22, Social Blade), about 700 new follows from ~2.7M plays.

5) Comments. Of the 96 comments read (out of 112), 11 accounts post memecoin "DM me" pitches (several carry TikTok's own downrank/duplicate flags), 14 are emoji- or sticker-only, 7 come from auto-numbered usernames, and one account was created 58 minutes before the video. Real engagement exists too (the top comment has 2,052 likes and mocks Kimchi), so the spam alone isn't proof of creator botting.

6) Context. This looks like a paid "Orangie" clip page: every clip is tagged #orangie, and the FOMO x ClipFarm campaign pays $1.25-2 per 1K views. Rasmr's bio carries a FOMO referral link. So even the genuine views measure a distribution campaign, not grassroots demand.

Limits: TikTok doesn't expose where views come from, and I could see only the newest 24 of 870 videos. This is strong circumstantial evidence, not proof.

Full analysis + data table: https://claude.ai/artifact/VqrYUs4LfW8p8gcpwvkQyN

claims.title: Kimchi TikTok: verified reach, unproven authenticity
claims.description:
Independent public-data audit, 24 Oct 2026, 18:00-18:02 UTC. ProMartY, Codex-assisted. @silence_inf

ANSWER: The clip has substantial displayed reach and relatively thin discussion. These public counters do not establish purchased views, automated likes, comment pruning or purely organic recommendation. They also do not establish a Kimchi fanbase.

DIRECT EVIDENCE. I opened the cited video through the logged-out @clipsbykes profile grid. Target https://www.tiktok.com/@clipsbykes/video/7698896779714071830 (Kimchi/Gunna, shown as 3 days old): 1.1M displayed views, 95.9K likes, 107 comments, 4,497 bookmarks. Bookmarks are NOT shares; shares were not measured. K/M figures are rounded. Grid and modal readings were within two minutes, not synchronized analytics.

CONTROLS, same account:
https://www.tiktok.com/@clipsbykes/video/7698902474559687938 (Kimchi UP UP, 3 days): 190.4K views / 7,998 likes / 27 comments / 724 bookmarks.
https://www.tiktok.com/@clipsbykes/video/7698907678969498902 (Kimchi Batman, 3 days): 284.6K / 29.7K / 111 / 1,565.
https://www.tiktok.com/@clipsbykes/video/7698057769068285206 (Cupsey, 6 days): 26.5K / 903 / 24 / 72.

Calculated from those displays: target likes/views about 8.72%, between the nearby Kimchi controls' 4.20% and 10.44%. Comments per 1,000 likes: target 1.12; controls 3.38 and 3.74. Bookmarks per 1,000 likes: target 46.89; controls 90.52 and 52.69. The comment gap is worth investigating, but these observations do not identify how the engagement was generated. The older Cupsey clip has 26.58 comments per 1,000 likes; treating that different topic/age as the universal baseline would confound the comparison.

REACH CONTEXT. I preserved 42 visible grid rows, including 2 pinned posts. In the 40 non-pinned rows, displayed views span 976 to 1.1M, median about 16,050; next-largest 400.6K. The target is about 2.75x the next-largest in this subset. This is a convenience sample, not the whole account or an age-normalized sample. An outlier is not a probability of fraud.

COMMENT CONTENT. Visible target comments include criticism, requests for the source vlog and personal memecoin-profit claims, rather than uniformly positive endorsements. A visible handle also posts a different profit claim under the Cupsey control. This weakens a blanket 'all enthusiastic fans' reading; it does not establish that the uploader bought activity or identify that commenter as a bot.

ATTRIBUTION. The clip combines Kimchi, Gunna and a luxury-purchase hook. Even organic views cannot isolate which person attracted the viewers or how many became Kimchi followers/customers.

LIMITS. No creator traffic-source/retention/unique-viewer/geography/promotion analytics, no defensible time series, and no complete commenter-identity audit. I cannot infer growth bursts, frozen counters, deleted comments, or a universal organic threshold. Saves can also be manipulated. Direct video navigation initially failed, while the profile-grid modal worked: a failed load is not proof of deletion. Other Poidh claimants' datasets and models were not used.

WHAT WOULD RESOLVE IT. Voluntarily shared traffic-source/promotion analytics and follower conversion, plus a fixed 24-hour counter comparison. Another public snapshot can measure displayed growth, not private provenance.

Conclusion: measurable viral reach, unresolved authenticity. Calling the engagement fraudulent from this evidence would overstate the result; equating one mixed-person clip with proof of a large Kimchi fanbase would also overstate it. Source screenshots and timestamped local captures were preserved; attached graphic summarizes these independent observations.

claims.title: The 871:1 ratio is a scaling fallacy — a 16-post audit
claims.description:
Short answer: the likes and saves look organic. The comment count is the only real anomaly, and it points to comment pruning, not bots.

DATA. 16 posts from @clipsbykes (2026-10-13 to 10-24), with likes / comments / saves / shares pulled from the public pages, publish times decoded from the video IDs. Target vector taken from the 2026-10-21 screenshot: 48,800 likes / 56 comments / 2,305 saves.

MODEL. Engagement on one account is not a constant rate, it scales with reach. I fitted the account's own scaling law:
  ln(comments) = -1.450 + 0.575 ln(likes)    R2 0.66, residual sd 0.80
  ln(saves)    = -1.652 + 0.888 ln(likes)    R2 0.96, residual sd 0.34

At 48,800 likes that predicts 116 comments (95% prediction interval 24-554) and 2,800 saves (1,450-5,405). Observed 56 and 2,305. Both are INSIDE the band: z = -0.92 (p = 0.18) and z = -0.58 (28th percentile).

WHY THE VIRAL TAKE IS WRONG. Comments on this account grow SUBLINEARLY with likes (exponent 0.575): a post with 10x the likes gets only about 3.5x the comments. So a 48.8K-like post is expected to show far fewer comments per like than a 500-like post. Comparing the two, which is exactly what the "48K likes, 56 comments, botted" threads did, is a scaling fallacy. The famous 871:1 ratio is what this account's own law predicts at this size.

WHY SAVES MATTER MORE THAN COMMENTS. A like panel does not produce saves. Across 15 posts spanning 56 to 29,100 likes, saves track likes with R2 = 0.96. If likes had been bought in bulk, saves would fall below that line. They do not: 2,305 against an expected 2,800.

THE ONE REAL OUTLIER. Saves per comment is 41.2, against an account median of 9.7 (p about 0.05). Saves normal plus comments low means comments were removed or hidden after the fact. That is the opposite of like-buying, which would have dragged saves down as well. So the anomaly is in the comment section, not in the audience.

CALIBRATION AGAINST A CONFIRMED CASE. Cai Xukun's 2018 Weibo post (Xingyuan app; operator arrested 2019, about 8M RMB profit) reached 100,000,000+ reposts, 2,400,000 comments and 1,060,000 likes. Reposts/likes = 94. Reposting costs strictly more than liking, so that ratio is structurally impossible at any scale, not merely unusual. This video violates no such constraint: every ratio it shows sits inside a range the account has produced before. The gap between unusual and impossible is the whole argument.

ROBUSTNESS. z between -0.58 and -1.36 across four specifications (OLS and Theil-Sen, full sample and dropping the three smallest posts). Nothing reaches |z| = 2.

CAVEATS I would want a reader to hold. (1) No view counts were obtainable, so the like/view test, the standard first-line check, could not be run. (2) The target video's short link now returns "Couldn't find this page", so it cannot be re-sampled and growth after 11 hours is unmeasured. (3) The within-account baseline assumes the account is mostly organic; if it is a paid asset, the reference class absorbs the manipulation and this test under-reports. That is why the tight saves fit matters, since proportional faking across 15 posts of wildly different sizes is hard. (4) n = 15 and comment counts are small integers, so the comment interval spans 24 to 554.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT. Like-to-view ratio; a second sample 24h later (organic keeps accruing, bought flatlines); a comment-content audit (uniformly positive surviving comments plus criticism visible on X equals pruning); audience geography (like panels are often geo-mismatched).

Full report with method, dataset table and code: ipfs://QmUv7XCdL1pgfC9e9xcRXNtGb5B2H5q9Zzdn83LFgCCexn

claims.title: 1.1M views, 102 comments: the Kimchi clip's engagement cannot be organic (13x below the account's own comment-per-like)
claims.description:
Measured 2026-10-24 ~05:30 UTC, public TikTok data only.

METHOD. 104 videos' view counters read from the public profile grid (real browser); exact published stats
(playCount, diggCount, commentCount, shareCount, collectCount, createTime) read from each video page's embedded
payload for 16 videos: the cited video, the 5 largest, and 10 spread across the range including the newest.

BASELINE, the same account's other 15 measured videos: likes/views median 3.63%, comments/views 0.057%,
comments/likes 1.42%, shares/views 0.236%.

THE CITED VIDEO (7698896779714071830, posted 2026-10-20, reached from the bounty's short link):
1,100,000 views; 93,900 likes = 8.54% (2.35x ABOVE baseline); 102 comments = 0.0093% (6.1x BELOW baseline);
comments/likes 0.109% (13.1x BELOW baseline); 1,436 shares = 0.131% (1.8x below).

WINDOW CHECK. The other six videos posted 18-23 Oct got 2,593 / 3,084 / 8,834 / 24,500 / 26,300 / 269,500 views,
median 16,667. The cited video sits in that same window at 1,100,000 = 66x the window median.

WHY THIS IS NOT ORGANIC. Organic virality lifts comments and shares together with views. Here likes ran 2.35x
above the account's own like rate while comment-per-like collapsed 13.1x and shares halved. The absolute
numbers name two different regimes: 102 comments is the level of the account's ~16,000-view videos, while
1,100,000 views and 93,900 likes are 66x and 150x above it. A view+like block of that size with conversation
left at a few-thousand-view scale is the signature of purchased views and likes, not of reach. Expected likes at
the account's own 3.63% on 1.1M views would be ~39,900; the video shows 93,900, i.e. likes were inflated too.
The same signature, about 3x weaker, appears on the 2026-10-21 video (269,500 views, 0.039% comments).

THE REST OF THE ACCOUNT LOOKS ORGANIC. The other 15 measured videos are normal: like rates 2.12-10.43%,
comment rates 0.03-0.21%, comment/like 0.37-8.51%. The anomaly is specific to the cited video.

LIMITS, STATED. TikTok does not expose watch time, retention, audience geography or traffic sources, so bought
views cannot be proven from outside; what can be shown is the internal inconsistency above. 104 of the
account's 866 videos were readable in the public grid, so the baseline is a sample of recent uploads. Profile
grid counters are rounded by TikTok; every number in the table comes from the individual video pages.

Full report, full 16-row table and reproduction steps: https://paste.rs/hvj7y

claims.description:

claims.title: analyze Kimchi posts on TikTok
claims.description:
The engagement on this video is highly inorganic. The likes are strongly suspected to be purchased, and the views are artificially inflated. The claim that this video represents organic, massive popularity is fundamentally unreliable.

To prove this, I compared the target video against the account's own historical baseline, analyzed the raw comment data (CSV), and evaluated the algorithmic inconsistencies.

1. Quantitative Anomaly (The Math)

· Target Video ("Kimchi & Gunna"): ~998,400 Views / 86,800 Likes / 95 Comments.
· Target Ratio: 913 Likes per 1 Comment.
· Account Baseline: I analyzed 3 other videos on @clipsbykes (Bottega, Pinned, and 45k bags). Their average like-to-comment ratio is ~150:1 (ranging from 73:1 to 261:1).
· The Red Flag: The target video's like-to-comment ratio is 6x higher than the account's normal average. Likes are the cheapest metric to buy; genuine conversations are not.

2. Qualitative Evidence (The "Smoking Gun" & Raw Data)
I extracted the full comment section (Raw CSV linked below) and found definitive proof of artificial inflation:

· The Top Comment Discrepancy: The video has 86,800 likes, but the most-liked comment on the entire video only has 1,754 likes. If 86K real, engaged humans liked this video, the top comments would have 10K+ likes. This massive gap proves the video likes did not come from an engaged audience (bots just click "like" and scroll away).
· Bot Spam: The comment section is flooded with obvious crypto scam bots (e.g., "Made $55k off memecoin", "Made 4k today", "Memecoins move fast. Being part of a solid alpha group...").
· Low-Effort Bot Comments: A large portion of the 95 comments are emoji-only replies (😳😳😳, 😂) with 0 to 2 likes, indicating fake accounts used to artificially inflate the comment count.

3. Algorithmic Inconsistency (Traffic Pool Theory)
TikTok's algorithm requires strong signals (comments and shares) to push a video from the test pools (200-500 users) to the viral tier (100K+ views). A video with ~1 million views but only 95 comments would never organically pass the algorithmic test pools. The views were clearly injected artificially to manufacture a "viral" look.

Conclusion:

claims.title: Kimchi clip on @clipsbykes: likes look bought, comments look real
claims.description:
Verdict: the likes on this clip do not look organic. Views are probably partly inflated too. The comment section itself looks real.

Data (public TikTok stats pulled Oct 23 2026 UTC). Target video 7698896779714071830, posted Oct 20: 998.4K views, 85.9K likes, 95 comments, 1,301 shares, 4,045 saves. Account @clipsbykes: 29K followers, 863 videos, 6.2M lifetime likes (about 7.2K per video), following 47.

Same-account baseline (other clipsbykes videos): "Bros going to school rich" 253.6K views / 6,050 likes / 133 comments; "Every time you HAVE to get out" 6,446 / 213 / 6; "She's actually getting really good" 5,601 / 139 / 2.

1) Like rate: target 8.6% of views vs 2.4% to 3.3% on the account's other clips (2.6x to 3.5x higher).
2) Likes per comment: target 904 to 1 vs 36 to 70 to 1 on the same account (13x to 25x). Organic TikTok usually sits around 30 to 150 likes per comment. A huge like count with almost no conversation is the classic signature of a bought like package, since likes are the cheapest metric to buy and comments are hard to fake convincingly.
3) Comments per view: 0.010% vs 0.036% to 0.093% baseline (4x to 10x lower). If 998K real people watched, you would expect roughly 350 to 900 comments at this account's normal rate, not 95. That points at some view padding as well.
4) Shares per view 0.13% and saves (4.7% of likes) are closer to normal, which suggests a real organic core under the padding.
5) Comment sample (48 of 95 pulled): on-topic memecoin chatter, spread naturally over 2 days, first comment about 2h after posting, plus the usual crypto scam spam ("made $55k", "alpha group"). No bot comment rings, so if botting happened it was likes/views, not comments.
6) Scale: this one clip has about 12x the account's average likes per video and about 1.4% of its lifetime likes in 2 days on a 29K follower clip page.

Caveat: public metrics cannot prove botting; a viral For You push can lower comment ratios somewhat. But a 900 to 1 like to comment ratio, far off this same account's own history, is the strongest red flag available from outside. Using this video as proof of Kimchi's massive TikTok popularity is not reliable.
